## Policies

### Peer Review

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| **Type** | Not conventional double-blind academic peer review. CPF has a named 'Reviewer Panel and Editorial Board' drawn from current DCP (Division of Clinical Psychology) members with 5+ years post-qualification experience; panel meets virtually ~3x/year and reviewers are credited by name monthly inside the cover. This reads as a practitioner/editorial-collective review model for a professional bulletin, not blinded external academic refereeing. A joint Clinical Editor + Managing Editor model is also mentioned in passing (source: WebSearch snippet of bps.org.uk page, page itself returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch so this is a secondary-source paraphrase, not primary-text confirmation). |
| **Transferable / Cascade?** | *(pending)* |
| **Reviewer reports published?** | *(pending)* |
| **Typical R+R rounds** | *(pending)* |
| **Reviewer recommendations** | *(pending)* |

> Source: https://www.bps.org.uk/clinical-psychology-forum-cpf-reviewer-panel-and-editorial-board

BPS has held general 'AI in psychological practice' conferences/policy workshops (topic-level, not an authorship rule), and BPS ran a 2025 cross-journal 'digital futures' Landmark Issue theme, but neither is an AI-use gate for authors/reviewers of CPF specifically. CPF is published directly on the BPS explore.bps.org.uk (HighWire) platform, not via Wiley, so Wiley's AI-for-authors guidance (used for BPS's Wiley-hosted journals like British Journal of Clinical Psychology) does not apply here without confirmation. |

**Current positioning (WO2, what the journal accepts now):** Practitioner-facing pieces from UK/Ireland clinical psychologists: brief research & evaluation papers (<=3000 words), reflective articles (<=2000 words), opinion pieces/position statements/research summaries (<=3500 words), reports of events, correspondence, book reviews, announcements, plus DCP policy/business updates. Recent (June 2025, issue 389) article titles found: 'The impact of imposter participants on psychology research', 'Reflections on supporting NHS hospital colleagues psychologically', and a piece on 'working with suicide' (evaluating service gaps) — indicating a mix of service evaluation, reflective/practice pieces, and methodological commentary rather than conventional empirical/quantitative research reports.

**Methods noted as welcome (WO2, qualitative — not a scored 0-5 table, see Methodological Preferences below):** service evaluation, reflective/practice commentary, qualitative/practice-based accounts, brief empirical research & evaluation papers, opinion/position pieces, book reviews, event reports
